title: Hope in mercy
hookLine: the late-night reel of every mistake, and the one thought the Prophet said to die with
tomorrow: what keeps working for you after you're gone?

cards: Late at night, the brain sometimes runs its worst-case reel: every mistake, every unsent apology, every prayer that slipped. It plays like evidence in a trial.
A report in Sahih Muslim names what should be on your mind at the very end, and it isn't the reel. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: let none of you die except thinking well of Allah.

teach.b: Thinking well of Allah, husn al-zann, means expecting good from Him: mercy, forgiveness, a welcome. Not because you've earned it, but because of who He is.

teach.h: AS MY SERVANT THINKS OF ME.
teach.b: A hadith qudsi in Sahih al-Bukhari, words the Prophet reports from Allah, puts it in one line: I am as My servant thinks of Me. Your picture of Allah is part of the meeting.
And the Qur'an speaks straight to people with real regrets.

It addresses those who have gone too far against themselves, and tells them, in Pickthall's words: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." Mercy is offered to exactly the people running the reel.

Some scholars describe fear and hope as two wings: fear keeps you careful while there's time to change. Some teachers add that near the end, hope should lead. None of this is permission to stop trying.
It's what to hold when the trying is mostly done, or when the reel won't stop playing. So the advice in this report isn't about a final deed. It's about a thought.

how: Muslims speak of husn al-zann, thinking well of Allah; those sitting with someone who is dying often speak to them of Allah's mercy, and Qur'an 39:53 is a verse people turn to when they fear they are beyond forgiveness.

o: expecting good from Allah, above all at the end
a prayer asking for mercy said only at funerals
being sure you've done enough good to be saved

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: I am as My servant thinks of Me
despair not of the mercy of Allah

s: thinking well of Allah means you can stop trying
it's what to hold when the trying is mostly done, or when regret won't stop. fear keeps you careful while there's time.
Qur'an 39:53 speaks to people who have gone too far against themselves
and tells exactly them: despair not of the mercy of Allah.
at the very end, Islam teaches you to focus on your sins so you can repent
in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: let none of you die except thinking well of Allah.

games.q: a friend who stopped practicing years ago tells you, 'after everything i've done, there's no way i'm forgiven.' which line from today speaks to exactly that?
o: despair not of the mercy of Allah, who forgiveth all sins.
fear and hope are like two wings on a bird.
be in this world like a stranger or a traveler.
games.why: 39:53 addresses people who went too far against themselves, and tells them not to despair. mercy is offered to exactly them.

practice: Count on your fingers the times you were met with kindness you didn't earn: a parent who forgave, a friend who stayed, a good thing that came anyway. Let each finger be one reason to think well.
Stop wherever you are when the time ends.

wordCard.voice: Hope in mercy: expecting good from Allah, especially at the end. Not a scorecard, but a trust in who He is.

orig.note: Arabic: good opinion, thinking well; here, expecting good from Allah.

carryVoice: For the late-night reel, two words: think well, because the verse says despair not. Rest easy tonight.
